lesson.title: When the condition changes

lead.text: Take the two coin flips from the last lesson. Before anything is known there are four equally likely outcomes. Now a friend peeks and tells you that at least one coin landed heads. That is a clue, and it changes what could have happened. TT has no heads in it, so it cannot be what happened. We cross it off.

Three outcomes survive: HH, HT and TH. They were equally likely before the clue. Crossing one off gives the others no advantage, so they stay equally likely. One of the three is two heads, which makes the chance of two heads 1 out of 3. Before the clue it was 1 out of 4.

A chance worked out inside the shorter list is called a conditional probability. Questions about one often use the word “given”: the chance of two heads, given at least one head. The clue sets the bottom of the fraction, and the outcomes you want are counted inside the shorter list.
A friend rolls a die out of your sight. She tells you only that the result is even. Cross off the results that the clue rules out.

The same thing happens on the grid of two dice. Suppose the clue is that the first die showed 1 or 2. Every pair whose first die is larger has been ruled out. The grid is built with the first roll down the side, so a clue about the first die removes whole rows.

afterFigure.text: The faded rows in the picture are the ones the clue has ruled out. Only the bright rows are still in play, and from now on everything is counted inside them. Those cells are the new list of possible outcomes, in the same way that HH, HT and TH were the new list for the coins.

lead.text: The first die is known to be 1 or 2. Count what is left in the grid.

reveal.text: Two rows of six cells remain. The clue changed the number of possible outcomes from 36 to the count you found.

lead.text: With the clue in place, 12 pairs can still have happened. Suppose we want the chance that the second die shows at most 4, given that the first showed 1 or 2. Look only at the surviving rows. Each row has four cells with a second roll of 1, 2, 3 or 4, so the two rows hold 8 matching pairs. The probability is 8 out of 12, which is 2/3.
The bottom of the fraction is 12, not 36. The 24 pairs in the crossed-off rows cannot have happened, so they have no place in the count.

afterFigure.text: A clue can keep other rows. “The first die is at least 5” keeps the bottom two rows and rules out the other four. The method is the same whichever rows survive: shrink the grid to the rows that fit the clue, count the pairs in them, then count the ones you want.

steps.headline: Given a first roll of at most 2, find the probability of a second roll of at most 3.

workedSteps.text: Two rows survive, so 12 pairs are possible.
Count the pairs in those rows with a second roll of at most 3.

lead.text: The clue and the question do not have to concern the same die. Keep the clue that the first die showed 1 or 2, and ask instead about the total. Suppose we want the chance of a total of at least 8.

In the first row, even a 6 on the second die only makes 7, so no pair there reaches 8. In the second row only (2,6) does. That is 1 pair out of the 12 that remain, which is 1/12. A small first die makes a high total hard to reach, and the number agrees.

afterFigure.text: The clue decides where to count. The event decides what to count there. Change either one and the answer changes, even though the grid underneath is the same.

lead.text: Now ask about a total of at least 7. Look only inside the rows the clue leaves, and divide by their pairs.
Suppose your friend gets a better look and says the first die was exactly 1. That is a tighter clue. Only the top row of the grid survives, so six pairs remain, one for each value of the second die.

afterFigure.text: In that row, the chance of a second roll of at most 3 is 3 out of 6, which is 1/2. A tighter clue leaves a shorter list, and each remaining pair carries more weight. All you need to ask is which second rolls fit the question.

lead.text: A tighter clue leaves less. The first die is known to be 1, so one row survives. Restrict first, then count the event inside it.

lesson.orientation: Restrict the possible outcomes before computing a conditional probability.
lesson.nextAction: Try a new case and return for recall after a delay.

blocks.text: A friend rolls two dice under a cup and keeps the cup down. You are asked to bet on whether the total is 7 or more. With nothing to go on, the grid of pairs from the last lesson gives you the answer. Then she lifts the cup for a moment and you catch sight of the first die. It was small, a 1 or a 2, but you could not tell which.
That glimpse should change your bet. A small first die makes a high total harder to reach, though it is hard to say by how much without working it out.

A clue like that adds nothing to the grid. It takes things away. Some pairs can no longer have happened, and the chances have to be worked out among the pairs that remain. This lesson shows how, first with two coins and then with the dice under the cup.

intro.promise: By the end you'll cross out the outcomes a clue rules out, and find a chance among the ones that remain.

recap.keyIdea: A clue shrinks the list of possible outcomes. A conditional probability counts the favourable outcomes inside the shorter list and divides by its size.

blocks.text: You cut 36 pairs down to 12 once you knew the first die was at most 2. Inside those rows, 6 pairs have a second roll of at most 3. Only 3 reach a total of at least 7. A tighter clue, a first roll of exactly 1, left a single row.

recap.nextHook: In every case so far a clue changed the chances. Sometimes a clue about one thing tells you nothing about another, as with a coin and a die. The next lesson starts there.

questions.prompt: You learn that the first roll is at most 2. How many ordered outcomes can still happen?
hints: Count only the two eligible rows.
The condition keeps two first-roll values; all second-roll values remain possible.
Multiply the two surviving rows by the six cells in each row.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two first-roll values remain, each with six second rolls: 2 × 6 = 12.

questions.onCorrect: 12. The clue removes whole rows; two rows of six pairs remain.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the grid before the clue. The clue crosses out whole rows.
That is one row. How many rows does the clue keep?

questions.prompt: Given a first roll of at most 2, what is the probability of a second roll of at most 3? Give a fraction or a decimal.
hints: Restrict both counts to the surviving rows.
Each eligible row has three matching second-roll values.
Divide two rows times three matches by two rows times six eligible values.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: There are 6 matching pairs among 12 eligible pairs, so 6/12 = 1/2.

questions.onCorrect: Half. Count inside the surviving rows: matches over the pairs the clue leaves.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by 36, the grid before the clue. Divide by what remains.
That counts matching pairs. A probability divides by the pairs still possible.

questions.prompt: Given a first roll of at most 2, what is the probability of a total of at least 7? Give a fraction or a decimal.
hints: Count pairs in the two eligible rows that sum to at least 7.
In the row for first roll 1, only second roll 6 qualifies. In row 2, second rolls 5 and 6 qualify.
Divide the three matching cells by the count in two complete eligible rows.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The matching pairs are (1,6), (2,5) and (2,6), so 3/12 = 1/4.

questions.onCorrect: A quarter. Look only in the two surviving rows, then divide by their 12 pairs.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts pairs in all six rows. The clue leaves only two.
That counts pairs. Divide by the pairs the clue leaves.

questions.prompt: Now the first roll is known to be 1. What is the probability that the total is 7? Give a fraction or a decimal to three places.
hints: A first roll of 1 fixes the row.
Only the first row remains; ask which second-roll value reaches the target.
One second-roll value qualifies among all six eligible second-roll values.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only (1,6) qualifies among the six possible pairs in the first row: 1/6.

questions.onCorrect: One of the six pairs in the surviving row. A tighter clue leaves a smaller list.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by 36. The clue leaves one row of pairs.
One pair qualifies, but more than one is still possible.

questions.prompt: The first roll is known to be 1. What is the probability that the total is at least 5? Give a fraction or a decimal.
hints: Which second rolls reach 5 when the first is 1?
Subtract the fixed first roll from the target sum to find the minimum second roll.
The qualifying second rolls are 4, 5 and 6; divide their count by all six possibilities.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The second roll must be 4, 5 or 6. Three of six eligible outcomes qualify: 1/2.

questions.onCorrect: Half. A second roll of 4, 5 or 6 reaches the total, out of six possible.

misconceptions.feedback: Other second rolls also reach the target. List which ones do.
Check the lowest second roll that reaches the target: a smaller one falls short.

questions.prompt: A clue rules out some outcomes. What goes on the bottom of the probability?
hints: The clue changes what is still possible.

acceptedIdeas: Only outcomes compatible with the clue
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Conditioning restricts the sample space to outcomes compatible with the clue. Count favourable outcomes within that same restricted set.

choices.label: Only outcomes compatible with the clue

questions.onCorrect: Count what is still possible. The denominator is the outcomes that fit the clue.

misconceptions.feedback: That denominator includes pairs the clue has ruled out, which cannot have happened.
Dividing favourable by favourable is always the same number. The denominator is everything still possible.

questions.prompt: Two coins are flipped. You are told that at least one landed heads. How many of the four results HH, HT, TH and TT could still have happened?
hints: Cross out any result with no heads in it.
Which of the four has no heads at all?
Take TT out of the list and count what is left.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: TT has no heads, so HH, HT and TH remain: 3.

questions.onCorrect: 3. The clue crossed out TT and left a shorter list. That list is where the next probability lives.

misconceptions.feedback: TT has no heads, so it cannot match the clue. Cross it out.
Check HH as well as the mixed results: which of the four fit the clue?

questions.prompt: Why divide by 12 and not by 36?
hints: Which pairs can still have happened once you know the first roll?

acceptedIdeas: The clue rules out the other pairs, so only 12 can have happened
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Once the first roll is known to be at most 2, only the pairs in those two rows are possible.

choices.label: The clue rules out the other pairs, so only 12 can have happened
Dividing by 36 gives a smaller number, which is safer

questions.onCorrect: The clue rules out the other pairs, so only the pairs in the surviving rows can have happened.

misconceptions.feedback: The denominator is whatever the clue leaves possible, and that changes with the clue.
A probability is not chosen to be small. It has to count what is actually possible.

questions.prompt: How many of the 12 remaining pairs have a second roll of at most 3?
hints: Look at one surviving row. How many second rolls are at most 3?
Each row has the same count. How many rows survive?
Multiply the matches in one row by the number of rows.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 3 matching second rolls in each of 2 rows: 3 × 2 = 6.

questions.onCorrect: 6. Count favourable pairs inside the surviving rows only.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one row. Two rows survive.
That is every remaining pair. Count only those with a second roll of at most 3.

questions.prompt: The first roll is at least 5. What is the probability that the total is at least 10? Give a fraction or a decimal to three places.
hints: Which first rolls does the clue allow? How many pairs is that?
List the pairs inside those rows that total 10 or more.
Count them and divide by the pairs the clue allows.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Rows 5 and 6 give 12 pairs. Totals of at least 10 come from (5,5), (5,6), (6,4), (6,5) and (6,6): 5 of 12.

questions.onCorrect: 5/12. Restrict to the two rows the clue allows, then count inside them.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by 36. The clue leaves only two rows.
That is the number of matching pairs. Divide by the pairs the clue leaves.

questions.prompt: A die is rolled and you are told the result is even. How many results can still have happened?
hints: Which results are even?
List the even numbers on a die.
Count the even numbers on the die.
questions.onCorrect: 3. The clue left a shorter list of results.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the list before the clue. The clue rules some out.
More than one even result is possible.

citations.claim: A clue rules out outcomes, and a probability found inside the shorter list is a conditional probability.
An even-roll clue leaves 2, 4 and 6 as the possible results.
A clue about the first die removes whole rows of the grid of ordered outcomes.
Knowing the first roll is at most 2 leaves two rows of six pairs.
A conditional probability counts favourable pairs inside the surviving rows and divides by the pairs the clue leaves; 8/12 here.
Six of the 12 remaining pairs have a second roll of at most 3.
With the first die at most 2, only (2,6) reaches a total of 8, so the conditional probability is 1/12.
Inside the two surviving rows, 3 of the 12 pairs make a total of at least 7.
A first roll of exactly 1 leaves one row, and 3 of its 6 pairs have a second roll of at most 3.
With the first roll fixed at 1, only a second roll of 6 makes a total of 7, so 1 out of 6.
Two first-roll values remain, each with six second rolls: 2 × 6 = 12.
There are 6 matching pairs among 12 eligible pairs, so 1/2.
The matching pairs are (1,6), (2,5) and (2,6), so 3/12 = 1/4.
Only (1,6) qualifies among the six pairs in the first row: 1/6.
The second roll must be 4, 5 or 6: three of six eligible outcomes, 1/2.
Conditioning restricts the sample space to outcomes compatible with the clue.
Three matching second rolls in each of two rows gives 6 pairs.
Rows 5 and 6 give 12 pairs; five of them total at least 10.
Given a clue, only outcomes compatible with it remain possible.
Only a second roll of 3 gives 4. One of the six eligible outcomes qualifies: 1/6.
Conditional probability restricts the possible outcomes to those compatible with the given event.
